course_title: An Introduction to Programming the Internet of Things (IoT)
chapter_title: Embedded Systems and IoT Design Considerations
chapter_summary:
Every IoT device is an embedded system — a computer designed for a specific purpose, embedded inside a larger device, and optimized for that purpose. A smart thermostat is an embedded system. A fitness tracker is an embedded system. An industrial vibration sensor is an embedded system. Understanding embedded systems is fundamental to IoT because the device layer is entirely composed of them.

An embedded system has four key components: a **processor** (to run the program), **memory** (to store the program and data), **input/output interfaces** (to connect sensors and actuators), and **software** (the firmware that controls the system). Unlike a general-purpose computer, an embedded system is not designed for the user to install and run arbitrary software. It runs one specific program, often forever, without a screen, keyboard, or mouse.

The processor in an embedded system can be a **microcontroller** (like the ATmega328P in the Arduino Uno), a **microprocessor** (like the ARM Cortex-A53 in the Raspberry Pi), or a **system-on-chip (SoC)** that combines processor, memory, and peripherals on a single chip. The choice of processor depends on the application requirements:

- **Microcontrollers (e.g., Arduino, ESP32, STM32):** Low cost, low power, simple control tasks. Ideal for reading sensors, controlling LEDs, and running simple logic. Cost: $2–$20. Power: milliwatts to hundreds of milliwatts.
- **Single-Board Computers (e.g., Raspberry Pi, BeagleBone):** Higher performance, can run a full operating system (Linux), connect to the internet, and process complex data. Ideal for edge gateways, web servers, and computer vision. Cost: $20–$100. Power: 1–10 watts.
- **SoC with Wireless (e.g., ESP32, nRF52):** Combines a microcontroller with built-in Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. Ideal for battery-powered IoT devices that need wireless connectivity. Cost: $3–$10. Power: very low in sleep mode.

IoT design involves constant trade-offs. Every decision you make affects the others:
- **Cost vs. Capability:** A Raspberry Pi is more capable than an Arduino but costs more and uses more power. For a simple temperature logger, an Arduino with a cheap sensor is the right choice. For a gateway that runs a web server and processes video, a Raspberry Pi is necessary.
- **Power vs. Performance:** A device running on a coin-cell battery must minimize power consumption. This means using a low-power microcontroller, sleeping between measurements, and transmitting data infrequently. A mains-powered device can use a more powerful processor and transmit continuously.
- **Wired vs. Wireless:** Wired connections (Ethernet, USB, serial) are reliable, fast, and secure but require physical cables. Wireless connections (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular) are flexible but consume more power, have limited range, and are subject to interference.
- **Security vs. Convenience:** Strong encryption and authentication require more processing power and memory, which increases cost and power consumption. A cheap IoT device might skip security to save money, creating vulnerabilities.
- **Response Time vs. Complexity:** A system that must respond in milliseconds (e.g., an emergency stop button) needs simple, predictable hardware and software. A system that can respond in seconds (e.g., a weather station) can use more complex processing.

**Response time** is a critical concept in IoT. It is the time between when the system receives an input and when it responds. For example, when you press a button on a smart light switch, the light should turn on within 100 milliseconds. If it takes 5 seconds, the system feels broken. Response time depends on the sensor reading time, the processing time, the network latency, and the actuation time. IoT designers must measure and optimize each component of the response time.

**Design metrics** for IoT systems include:
- **Unit cost:** the manufacturing cost of the device.
- **Power consumption:** the average energy used per day (critical for battery-powered devices).
- **Size and weight:** important for wearables and embedded applications.
- **Reliability:** the mean time between failures (MTBF).
- **Security:** the resistance to hacking and data breaches.
- **Scalability:** the ability to add more devices without redesigning the system.

screens.title: Embedded Systems and IoT Design Considerations
screens.subtitle: How device-level choices shape power, cost, connectivity, and responsiveness

narration.text: In this lesson we will treat every IoT device as an embedded system — a purpose-built computer inside a larger product. You will learn the four hardware and software building blocks that make a device work, the main processor options you can choose from, and the trade-offs that drive those choices. We'll use concrete, everyday examples: a battery-powered soil sensor, a smart home gateway, and a wearable fitness tracker to show how power, cost, and connectivity influence design. I will also guide you through response time: what adds delay, what designers measure, and how to meet millisecond-level requirements when needed. By the end of this chapter you should be able to pick a processor category for a given scenario and justify that choice using at least two trade-offs such as power versus performance or cost versus capability. Notice common misconceptions as we go — for example, more capability is not always better for a battery-powered sensor. Keep that practical tension in mind as you explore the topics below. What device are you most likely to design, and which trade-off will matter first?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Every IoT device is an embedded system. Choose processors and connectivity by balancing cost, power, size, security, and response time to meet real-world constraints.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives focus your work on practical decision making. First, you will define what an embedded system is and explain how it forms the device layer of the IoT. That means you can identify components such as processor, memory, input/output interfaces, and firmware in a real product. Second, you will compare microcontrollers, microprocessors, and single-board computers and match each to common IoT roles. For each comparison you'll use concrete factors like cost, power draw, and whether the device runs a full operating system. Third, you will practice evaluating design trade-offs: how cost competes with capability, and how power constraints influence hardware selection. You will learn to state which trade-offs matter first for a scenario. Fourth, you will identify the key constraints — power, cost, size, connectivity, security, and response time — and explain how each one narrows hardware choices. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can check your reasoning with hands-on scenarios.

narration.text: Now let's translate those objectives into applied practice. You will be able to pick a microcontroller for a long-life sensor and justify that choice by explaining power-saving tactics such as deep-sleep and infrequent transmissions. You will explain why a single-board computer is chosen for gateways that run dashboards and aggregate data. You will evaluate wired and wireless options and argue for Ethernet or LoRa depending on reliability, range, and power needs. Finally you will measure response time by identifying sensor read, processing, network, and actuation segments and explain how each segment contributes to delays. These applied skills are critical because engineering decisions are rarely about a single metric; they are about trade-offs. A checkpoint exercise at the end asks you to select hardware for a soil sensor and defend your choices with two trade-offs. That exercise maps directly to the competency milestones in the first objectives screen.

screens.title: What is an Embedded System?
screens.subtitle: Definition, core components, and why they differ from general-purpose computers

narration.text: An embedded system is a computer designed for one specific purpose, built into a larger device and optimized to perform that role reliably. Core components are a processor to run the program, memory to store code and data, input/output interfaces to connect sensors and actuators, and the software — often called firmware — that controls behaviors. Unlike a laptop or desktop, embedded systems rarely accept arbitrary applications; they run a single program for long periods and often lack a keyboard or display. Consider a smart thermostat: it reads temperature sensors, runs control logic, and operates a heating relay. That same structure appears in a fitness tracker or an industrial vibration sensor. A common misconception is to assume embedded systems must be tiny or weak; embedded systems vary in capability depending on requirements, but their defining trait is purpose-driven design. Example: a soil-moisture sensor needs a simple processor, minimal memory, and low-power radios to sleep for long periods. Key takeaway: identify the four components and ask how each one affects power, cost, and response time when you evaluate a design. What is an Embedded System? means an embedded system is a purpose-built computer with processor, memory, i/o, and firmware optimized for a single task.. In practical terms, definition, core components, and why they differ from general-purpose computers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: An embedded system is a purpose-built computer with processor, memory, I/O, and firmware optimized for a single task.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is an Embedded System?
Definition
An embedded system runs a dedicated program to perform one role inside a larger device. It is optimized across processor, memory, interfaces, and firmware to meet constraints like power and response time.
Processor
Runs control logic and computation.
Memory
Stores firmware and transient data.
I/O
Connects sensors and actuators.
Software
Firmware that runs continuously and predictably.
Key Takeaway

Embedded systems are defined by purpose and constraints, not size alone. Use their component roles to evaluate hardware choices.

Concrete example: soil moisture sensor
A buried moisture sensor typically uses a low-power microcontroller, small flash memory for firmware, an ADC input for the sensor, and a radio that wakes periodically to transmit. The entire unit must minimize average power to meet battery life targets.
Common misconception
More processing capability is always better. In fact, extra capability increases cost and power, which can ruin a battery-powered design.
Why this matters: once you can name the four components, you can reason about trade-offs. For a millisecond critical task, pick simpler hardware to reduce unpredictability. For heavy data processing, choose a device that can run a full OS.

screens.title: Microcontroller vs. Single-board Computer vs. SoC
screens.subtitle: How processor classes map to IoT roles and constraints

narration.text: Choosing between a microcontroller, a single-board computer, and a system-on-chip with wireless is one of the most frequent decisions in IoT design. Microcontrollers like Arduino-class chips are low cost and low power; they excel at simple sensing and control tasks and can run for long periods on batteries. Single-board computers, such as Raspberry Pi-class devices, run a full operating system and provide high performance for gateways, dashboards, and local processing, but they cost more and draw more power. SoCs with wireless — examples include ESP32 and nRF52 — combine a controller with integrated Wi‑Fi or Bluetooth and are ideal for battery-powered wireless devices. Use cost, power, and capability as your axes: microcontrollers are lowest cost and power with limited capability, SBCs are high capability and higher power, and SoCs sit in the middle with built-in radios. A concrete example: use an MCU for a temperature logger, an SBC for a home gateway that serves a local dashboard, and an SoC for a wearable that needs Bluetooth. Misconception check: don’t pick an SBC simply because it is familiar; its power profile may be incompatible with battery life requirements. What trade-offs will your current project force you to prioritize?

keyIdea.title: Processor mapping
keyIdea.text: Microcontrollers: low cost/power. SBCs: high capability, high power. SoCs: integrated wireless, balanced for battery use.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Processor Comparison
Quick comparison cards
Microcontroller (MCU)
Low cost, milliwatt power, ideal for simple sensors and actuators. Example cost range: low dollars.
Single-board computer (SBC)
Higher performance, runs Linux, suitable for gateways and heavy processing. Consumes watts and costs more.
SoC with wireless
Includes Wi‑Fi or Bluetooth on a microcontroller-class chip, balancing low power and connectivity for battery devices.
Misconception
Assuming a single processor class fits all cases. Instead, match the class to cost, power, and capability needs of the scenario.
Scenario mappings
Microcontroller: simple temperature logger, event counters, LED control. SBC: local dashboard, protocol gateway, computer vision prototype. SoC+wireless: wearable fitness tracker, battery sensors needing Wi‑Fi or Bluetooth.
Example justification
If you must run for 7 days on one charge, avoid SBCs. If you need local web serving and protocol bridging for 50 sensors, prefer an SBC for CPU and memory headroom.
Key Takeaway

Match hardware class to role: conserve power with MCUs, get capability with SBCs, or choose SoCs for built-in wireless and balanced power.

screens.title: Design Trade-offs: Cost, Power, and Capability
screens.subtitle: A stepwise approach to weigh conflicting constraints

narration.text: Designing an IoT device is primarily an exercise in trade-offs. Use a simple stepwise process to make these decisions explicit. Step one: list the non-negotiable requirements — battery life target, maximum unit cost, required response time, and necessary connectivity. Step two: rank those requirements by priority because some trade-offs are impossible to meet simultaneously. Step three: map processor classes and wireless options to the ranked requirements. For instance, if battery life and unit cost are highest priority, a microcontroller with a low-power radio is likely the right fit. Step four: identify implementation tactics such as aggressive sleep modes, batching network transmissions, or moving processing to a gateway. Step five: validate by estimating metrics — average power consumption, response time budget, and unit cost. A concrete example: for a soil sensor required to run two years on battery and transmit every six hours, prioritize power and choose a low-power MCU with a low-duty-cycle radio or long-range low-power protocol. A common error is trying to optimize everything at once; instead accept trade-offs and iterate. The key is to turn vague constraints into quantitative targets and derive hardware from them.

keyIdea.title: Decision process
keyIdea.text: Convert requirements into ranked priorities, map hardware options, apply power-saving tactics, then validate with metric estimates.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Design Trade-offs
Five-step decision flow
  1. List non-negotiable requirements and metrics.
  2. Rank requirements by priority.
  3. Map processor and radio options to priorities.
  4. Choose tactics: sleep modes, batching, offload processing.
  5. Estimate metrics and validate choices.
Concrete scenario
Soil moisture sensor: requirement — two-year battery life, transmit every six hours. Prioritize power and size. Choose a low-power microcontroller, use deep-sleep between readings, and a low-duty-cycle long-range radio to minimize transmit energy.
Common-mistake
Optimizing for capability first leads to selecting processors that consume too much power. Always test the estimated daily energy budget before choosing an SBC for a battery design.
Key Takeaway

Follow a stepwise process: requirements → ranking → hardware mapping → tactics → validation. That converts trade-offs into engineering choices.

screens.title: Wired vs. Wireless Connectivity
screens.subtitle: Reliability, power, range, and when to choose each

narration.text: Connectivity choices are central to IoT design and carry clear trade-offs. Wired options such as Ethernet or USB provide reliability, consistent bandwidth, and lower security exposure because physical access is required. They are appropriate where power and stable links are available. Wireless options — Wi‑Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, or low-power long-range protocols — offer flexibility and ease of installation but generally consume more power and are subject to interference and variable latency. Choose wired connectivity when latency, security, and throughput are critical and cabling is feasible. Select wireless for battery devices, mobile nodes, or when physical cabling is impossible. A concrete contrast: a factory sensor that must stream high-frequency vibration data might use wired Ethernet for reliability and low latency, while a distributed soil sensor network that needs long battery life will favor a low-power wireless link and infrequent transmissions. A common error is assuming wireless always reduces cost; in many cases, higher battery or radio costs can offset the savings from avoiding cabling. The practical skill is to enumerate range, power, and reliability needs, then map them to wired or wireless choices.

keyIdea.title: Connectivity rule
keyIdea.text: Pick wired for reliability and low latency when feasible; pick wireless for flexibility and mobility but plan for power and interference trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Wired vs Wireless
Wired
  • Reliable and low-latency.
  • Lower exposure to RF interference.
  • Requires physical cabling and often mains power.
Use when uptime and latency are critical, or when devices are stationary with power available.
Wireless
  • Flexible installation and mobility.
  • Consumes more power and is subject to interference.
  • Range varies: Bluetooth short, Wi‑Fi medium, cellular and LoRa long.
Use when cabling is impractical or devices must be battery-operated or mobile.
Concrete example
Factory vibration sensor: choose wired Ethernet for reliable, continuous streaming. Soil sensors: choose low-power wireless with infrequent transmissions.
Common-mistake
Assuming wireless always lowers total cost. Consider battery size, replacement frequency, and radio costs before deciding.

screens.title: Power vs. Performance: Strategies for Low-Power IoT
screens.subtitle: Tactics to extend battery life while meeting functional needs

narration.text: Power management is often the single most important constraint for battery-operated IoT devices. Begin by calculating an energy budget: estimate active power for sensing, processing, and transmitting, and estimate sleep power. Use duty-cycling to minimize the proportion of time spent in active, high-power modes. Deep sleep modes on microcontrollers can reduce power consumption to microamps; wake only when needed for a reading or an event. Batch data and reduce transmission frequency to save radio energy. Choose radios and protocols that match the range and energy profile — integrated SoCs with optimized sleep modes are often the best choice for Bluetooth or Wi‑Fi light use. Another tactic is to offload heavy computation to a gateway or cloud so the device remains simple and low-power. A concrete example: a wearable that must last seven days might sample sensors at a lower rate, compress or summarize data before sending, and use BLE for occasional syncs versus continuous Wi‑Fi. A common misconception is that lowering sample rate always harms value; instead, consider event-triggered sensing and adaptive sampling to preserve useful information while saving energy. The key is to measure and iterate: estimate, implement low-power tactics, measure actual consumption, and refine.

keyIdea.title: Power tactics
keyIdea.text: Use duty-cycling, deep sleep, batching, and offloading to meet battery targets while keeping required functionality.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Power vs Performance
Step-by-step tactics
  • Estimate active and sleep power.
  • Duty-cycle sensors and radios.
  • Use deep sleep and wake on event.
  • Batch transmissions and compress data.
  • Offload heavy processing to a gateway.
Concrete example: 7-day wearable
Reduce sampling rate during rest, summarize data hourly, use BLE for sync, and put main MCU in deep sleep between samples to meet a multi-day battery life.
Common-mistake
Assuming hardware sleep modes are automatic. Sleep behavior is implemented in firmware and must be validated with real measurements.
Key Takeaway

Quantify energy, reduce active duty, and validate with measurements. Firmware strategies are as important as hardware selection.

screens.title: Response Time in IoT Systems
screens.subtitle: Breaking down sensor read, processing, network, and actuation delays

narration.text: Response time is the time between when a system receives an input and when it performs the required output. In IoT it is useful to break response time into segments: sensor read time, processing time, network latency, and actuation time. Sensor read time includes ADC conversion or sensor-specific sampling delays. Processing time is the firmware or software latency to compute a result. Network latency covers the stack: radio wake-up, transmission, routing, and potential cloud processing. Actuation time is the delay for the physical actuator to respond. Consider a smart light switch: the press-to-light interval should be under 100 milliseconds for a seamless user experience. If sensor read is 5 ms, processing 10 ms, network 60 ms, and actuation 25 ms, the system feels slow. Designers must measure each component, find the largest contributors, and optimize them — for example, reduce network hops, use local processing to avoid cloud round-trips, or select radios with faster wake times. Misconception: optimizing a single segment guarantees low total latency. In practice you must optimize the dominant segments and measure the end-to-end stack to be sure.

keyIdea.title: Response time
keyIdea.text: Response time is the sum of sensor read, processing, network, and actuation delays. Optimize the dominant segments for predictable behavior.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Response Time
Response time segments
Sensor read
ADC or sensor sampling delay
Processing
Firmware compute time
Network
Radio wake, transmission, routing
Actuation
Physical mechanism response
Example budget: sensor 5 ms, processing 10 ms, network 60 ms, actuation 25 ms → total 100 ms. To hit a tighter goal, identify the largest contributors and optimize them: move processing local, reduce network hops, or select faster radios.
Concrete scenario
Smart door unlock: requirement under 500 ms. Focus on fast sensor read, local processing for fingerprint verification, and low-latency actuation to meet the constraint.
Misconception
Optimizing only sensor speed may not help if network latency dominates. Always measure end-to-end.

screens.title: Design Metrics: Cost, Power, Size, Reliability, Security, Scalability
screens.subtitle: Quantify what matters when evaluating an IoT design

narration.text: Design metrics turn qualitative goals into numbers you can optimize. Unit cost is the manufacturing cost per device and directly affects business viability for large deployments. Power consumption — often reported as average energy per day — is critical for battery lifetimes. Size and weight matter for wearables and embedded installations. Reliability, often summarized as mean time between failures, tells you how often devices will require maintenance. Security is measured in resistance to breaches, the ability to update firmware, and use of encryption and authentication. Scalability describes whether the design can grow to more devices without redesign. When evaluating a design, always set target values: maximum unit cost, minimum battery life, acceptable MTBF, and required update capability. For example, a farm soil sensor that must run two years on battery sets a strict power target; that rules out SBCs. A gateway serving 50 sensors has a scalability and processing metric that favors an SBC. Misconceptions include treating these metrics as independent: improving one often degrades another. The practical skill is to list targets, trace each metric to hardware and software choices, and quantify the expected outcome before prototyping.

keyIdea.title: Metrics matter
keyIdea.text: Set numeric targets for cost, power, reliability, security, and scalability; use them to eliminate unsuitable hardware early.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Design Metrics
Unit cost
Affects feasibility for large deployments. Set a maximum per device early.
Power consumption
Express as average energy per day or expected battery life for the chosen battery.
Size & weight
Critical for wearables and embedded installations.
Reliability
Use MTBF estimates and field test data when possible.
Security
Measure the device's ability to authenticate, encrypt, and receive secure updates.
Scalability
Can the design be deployed at scale without redesign? Consider network load and provisioning.
Key Takeaway

Convert qualitative needs into numeric targets for cost, power, reliability, security, and scalability to guide hardware and firmware choices.

screens.title: Security vs. Convenience
screens.subtitle: Why stronger security often raises cost and power requirements

narration.text: Security is essential but it has a cost. Strong encryption and authentication require C P U cycles, memory for keys and certificates, and sometimes persistent storage for secure elements. Those resources increase unit cost and can raise power consumption, especially if cryptography is performed frequently. For IoT devices with constrained resources, designers must balance security requirements with power and cost constraints. For example, secure firmware updates require a secure boot chain and sufficient flash to store update images; that hardware overhead must be budgeted early. A common weak approach is to skip security to save money — this leaves devices vulnerable and can lead to larger costs in remediation. A practical approach is to implement security to the level required by the threat model: use lightweight cryptographic libraries when possible, offload heavy crypto to a gateway, and ensure an update path for future patches. Concrete example: a soil sensor should authenticate to the backend and use ephemeral session keys, but it may use a lightweight handshake to minimize computation. The key is to document the threat model and allocate resources to the protections that matter most.

keyIdea.title: Security trade-off
keyIdea.text: Security increases compute, memory, and sometimes power needs. Design security to match the threat model and budget resources accordingly.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Security vs Convenience
Security cost components
  • CPU cycles for cryptography.
  • Memory for keys, certificates, and secure storage.
  • Flash space for secure updates and rollback protection.
Designers must budget these resources and choose lightweight protocols when hardware is constrained or offload to a gateway when possible.
Concrete example
A remote sensor should authenticate to the server using lightweight handshakes and maintain an update mechanism. Avoid disabling security to save a few dollars.
Common-mistake
Designers assume security can be added later without hardware changes. In many constrained devices, hardware limits make later additions infeasible.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity and Assessment Guidance
screens.subtitle: Practice selecting hardware and defending design trade-offs

narration.text: Apply what you've learned to concrete device scenarios. For each scenario, list the top two constraints and use them to pick a processor and connectivity option. Example scenarios include: a wearable fitness tracker needing seven-day battery life; a smart home gateway for fifty ZigBee sensors and a local dashboard; an industrial monitor powered by solar and sending hourly cellular reports; and a smart door lock requiring sub-500 millisecond unlock latency. For the wearable, prioritize power and size, pick a low-power SoC with Bluetooth, and use deep-sleep. For the gateway, prioritize capability and scalability, choose a single-board computer to run a local dashboard and protocol bridging. For the industrial monitor, choose a low-power microcontroller with a cellular link or low-power wide-area network depending on range; account for solar charging and duty cycle. For the door lock, prioritize response time and predictability: use simple, local processing and low-latency radios or wired actuation. Assessment idea: design a buried soil moisture sensor that must run two years on battery and transmit every six hours. Choose a processor and wireless protocol, then explain why a Raspberry Pi is a poor fit. Your justification should cite power and cost metrics.

keyIdea.title: Practice activity
keyIdea.text: Select hardware for scenarios, justify choices with two trade-offs, and validate by comparing expected power, cost, and response time against targets.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Hands-on Activity
Activity instructions
For each given scenario, do the following: 1) State the top two constraints, 2) Choose processor class and wireless option, 3) Explain two trade-offs justifying the choice, and 4) Estimate impact on power, cost, or response time.
Scenario A: Wearable fitness tracker
Prioritize power and size. Choose a low-power SoC with BLE and deep-sleep to meet seven-day life.
Scenario B: Smart home gateway
Prioritize capability and scalability. Choose an SBC to run a local dashboard and bridge many ZigBee nodes.
Scenario C: Industrial solar monitor
Prioritize power and range. Choose an MCU with long-range low-power radio and plan for energy harvesting constraints.
Scenario D: Smart door lock
Prioritize response time and predictability. Use simple local processing and fast actuation; test end-to-end latency.
Assessment idea
Design a buried soil sensor requiring two-year battery life and 6-hour reporting. Choose a processor and wireless protocol, and explain why a Raspberry Pi is unsuitable due to power and cost.
Pro tip
Always estimate a daily energy budget and test with real hardware early to avoid late design surprises.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Essential definitions and comparisons to remember

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important concepts. First, an embedded system is a purpose-built computer consisting of processor, memory, input/output, and firmware. Second, microcontrollers are low cost and low power, suited for simple sensing and control tasks. Third, single-board computers run full operating systems and are appropriate for gateways and local processing but consume more power. Fourth, SoCs with integrated wireless provide a balance by combining an MCU with Wi‑Fi or Bluetooth for battery devices. These ideas are the foundation for every hardware decision you will make in IoT. Keep these comparisons in your head when you map requirements to hardware choices later in exercises. A final reminder: capability and power often pull in opposite directions, so choose the smallest platform that meets your requirements. Which of these core ideas will guide your next design choice?

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Embedded system components and the three processor archetypes form the base for IoT hardware decisions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Key Concepts
Embedded system
Processor, memory, I/O, and firmware optimized for one task.
Microcontroller
Low cost and low power for simple sensing and control.
SBC & SoC
SBCs run full OS and are powerful; SoCs combine MCU and wireless for battery devices.
Summary

Use these core distinctions to start every design: identify constraints, then pick the processor and connectivity that satisfy them.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs, response time, and design metrics in brief

narration.text: Finish with the practical reminders you will return to often. Trade-offs are unavoidable: cost vs capability, power vs performance, wired vs wireless, and security vs convenience. Response time is the sum of sensor read, processing, network, and actuation delays, and meeting tight latency goals means optimizing the dominant segments. Design metrics — unit cost, power consumption, size, reliability, security, and scalability — should be turned into numeric targets early. Use a checklist when evaluating hardware: can it meet the power budget, does it offer required connectivity, and can it be secured and updated? Finally, validate choices by prototyping and measuring; many assumptions break when tested with real hardware. Keep these short rules of thumb handy as you design devices and run the hands-on activity to practice justifying your choices with two trade-offs each time.

keyIdea.title: Practical rules
keyIdea.text: Always define numeric targets, accept trade-offs, and prototype early to validate assumptions about power, latency, and cost.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Key Concepts
Trade-offs
Design decisions require explicit trade-offs; list and rank them early.
Response time
Measure sensor, processing, network, and actuation times to meet latency goals.
Design metrics
Turn needs into numbers: cost, power, size, reliability, security, scalability.
Final takeaway

Document requirements quantitatively, choose hardware that meets them, and validate with prototypes and measurements.
